implementation_notes: Swift overloads + for its own types, so the additive monoids (Array, String, Set-adjacent) are built in, and a domain type's instance is an operator overload plus a static identity. Collection's reduce(_:) requires an initialValue, which makes the identity explicit. The performance traps are the standard ones: String + in a loop copies the whole buffer each time (reserveCapacity up front or accumulate into [String] and join), and Array + copies. Swift's value semantics make the aggregate cheap to copy, which is what makes the monoid laws hold by construction - there is no aliasing to worry about.
idiom_name: operator + overload plus static identity; reduce(_:) with an explicit initial value
pitfalls: String + in a loop copies the entire buffer each iteration; reserveCapacity or accumulate into an array and use joined().
Array + copies both operands; flatten once instead of folding with +.
reduce without an initialValue traps at runtime on an empty sequence - the identity case is exactly where the missing seed hurts.
Floating-point + is not associative, so a parallel reduction over Double changes the result relative to a sequential one.
